10        II.  LEGAL STANDARDS                                             
11             A.  Motion to Disqualify and Implied Waiver                 
12        The decision whether to disqualify counsel is committed to the discretion of the district 
13   court.  See Gas-A-Tron of Ariz. v. Union Oil Co. of Cal., 534 F.2d 1322, 1325 (9th Cir. 1976).  
14   State law is applied in determining matters of disqualification.  In re Cnty. of L.A., 223 F.3d 990, 
15   995 (9th Cir. 2000).  Generally, outright disqualification is disfavored because it may drastically 
16   affect several important interests—a client’s right to choose counsel, an attorney’s interest in 
17   representing a client, the financial burden on a client who must replace disqualified counsel, and 
18   the possibility that the disqualification motion is merely pursued for tactical reasons.  Concat LP v. 
19   Unilever, PLC, 350 F. Supp. 3d 796, 814 (N.D. Cal. 2004).             
20        “It is well settled that a former client who is entitled to object to an attorney representing 
21   an opposing party on the ground of conflict of interest but who knowingly refrains from asserting 
22   it promptly is deemed to have waived that right.”  Trust Corp. of Montana v. Piper Aircraft Corp., 
23   701 F.2d 85, 87 (9th Cir. 1983).  “Delay is significant not only from the perspective of prejudice 
24   to the nonmoving party, it is also an indication that the alleged breach of confidentiality was not 
25   seen as serious or substantial by the moving party.”  Liberty Nat’l Enter., L.P. v. Chi. Title Ins. 
26   Co., 194 Cal. App. 4th 839, 847 (2011).  If the opposing party “offers prima facie evidence of an 
27

1   unreasonable delay by the former client in making a motion and resulting prejudice to the current 
2   client,” the burden “shifts back to the party seeking disqualification to justify the delay.”  River 
3   W., Inc. v. Nickel, 188 Cal. App. 3d 1297, 1298 (1987).  That party should address “how long he 
4   has known of the potential conflict; whether he has been represented by counsel since he has 
5   known of the potential conflict; whether anyone prevented the moving party from making the 
6   motion earlier, and if so, under what circumstances; and whether an earlier motion to disqualify 
7   would have been inappropriate or futile, and why.”  Id. at 1309.      
8             B.  California Rule of Professional Conduct 1.18            
9        Pursuant to Civil Local Rule 11, every attorney practicing before this court must “comply 
10   with the standards of professional conduct required of members of the State Bar of California.”  
11   N.D. Cal. Civ. L.R. 11-4(a)(1).  Under California Rule of Professional Conduct 1.18, an attorney 
12   has a continued duty of confidentiality and loyalty to a potential client.  A “prospective client” is a 
13   person who consults a lawyer “for the purpose of retaining the lawyer or securing legal advice or 
14   advice from the lawyer in the lawyer’s professional capacity.”  Cal. R. Prof. Conduct 1.18(a).  
15   However, not all persons who communicate information to a lawyer are entitled to protection 
16   under this rule.  A person who “communicates information unilaterally to a lawyer, without 
17   reasonable expectation that the lawyer is willing to discuss the possibility of forming a lawyer-
18   client relationship or provide legal advice is not a ‘prospective client.’”  Id. cmt. 2.  Further, Rule 
19   1.18 only prohibits a material adverse representation if the lawyer received information from the 
20   prospective client that is protected by Business and Professions Code § 6068(e).  Id. 1.18(c).   
21        Business and Professions Code § 6068(e) covers “any information obtained by the lawyer 
22   during the professional relationship, or relating to the representation, which the client has 
23   requested to be inviolate or the disclosure of which might be embarrassing or detrimental to the 
24   client.”  State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct, 
25   Formal Opinion No. 2016-195 (cleaned up).  If the allegedly confidential information disclosed 
26   “becomes a matter of public record or is disclosed to third parties, the disqualification movant 
27                                                                         
    Case No.: 5:21-cv-04657-EJD                                           
1   cannot rely on such disclosures as confidential information.”  Faraday&Future, Inc. v. EVelozcity, 
2   Inc., 2018 WL 4849704, at *7 (C.D. Cal. May 30, 2018).                
3             C.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6)                
4        “To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, 
5   accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 
6   662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)).  A plaintiff must 
7   “plead[] factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is 
8   liable for the misconduct alleged[,]” which requires “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant 
9   has acted unlawfully.”  Id. (citing Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556).  These standards apply to both 
10   allegations in a complaint and in counterclaims.  See Starr v. Baca, 652 F.3d 1202, 1216 (9th Cir. 
11   2011).                                                                
12        Although “a court must accept as true all of the allegations contained in a complaint[,]” 
13   “[t]hreadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, supported by mere conclusory 
14   statements, do not suffice.”  Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 (citing Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).  “[T]o be 
15   entitled to [a] presumption of truth, allegations in a . . . counterclaim may not simply recite the 
16   elements of a cause of action, but must contain sufficient allegations of underlying facts to give 
17   fair notice and to enable the opposing party to defend itself effectively.”  Starr, 652 F.3d at 1216.  
18   Such factual allegations “must plausibly suggest an entitlement to relief, such that it is not unfair 
19   to require the opposing party to be subjected to the expense of discovery and continued litigation.”  
20   Id.                                                                   
21        “[A] plaintiff cannot assert a plausible claim for infringement under the Iqbal/Twombly 
22   standard by reciting the [patent] claim elements and merely concluding that the accused product 
23   has those elements.  There must be some factual allegations that, when taken as true, articulate 
24   why it is plausible that the accused product infringes the patent claim.”  Bot M8 LLC v. Sony Corp. 
25   of Am., 4 F.4th 1342, 1353 (Fed. Cir. 2021).  “A plaintiff is not required to plead infringement on 
26   an element-by-element basis.”  Id. at 1352 (citing Nalco Co v. Chem-Mod, LLC, 883 F.3d 1337, 
27

1   1350 (Fed. Cir. 2018)).  However, a plausible claim requires at least some allegations regarding 
2   how an accused product satisfies certain claim limitations.  See id. at 1355 (“While Bot M8 points 
3   to different storage components in the allegedly infringing devices, it never says which one or 
4   ones satisfy the mutual authentication limitation.”).                 
5        III.  DISCUSSION                                                 
6             A.  Defendants’ Motion to Disqualify Counsel                
7        To the extent a conflict exists, Defendants have waived their right to pursue it.  A 
8   chronology of this case is helpful.  On May 5, 2021, Baker Botts sent a letter informing 
9   Defendants that Baker Botts and Mr. Guy were representing QuickLogic in this matter.  See Dkt 
10   1-4.  Subsequently, on June 16, 2021, Plaintiff filed suit, listing “G. Hopkins Guy III” as counsel 
11   of record on its Complaint.  See Dkt. No.1.  Thereafter, in August 2021, Defendants moved to 
12   dismiss Plaintiff’s actions.  Mr. Guy, among other attorneys from Baker Botts, defended Plaintiff 
13   from dismissal.  See Dkt. No. 27.  It was not until nearly seven months into litigation, and after a 
14   failed motion to dismiss, that Defendants made any suggestion that grounds for disqualification 
15   existed.  See Dkt. No. 39 (filed February 8, 2022).  This delay is unreasonable as a matter of law.  
16   See, e.g., Skyy Spirits, LLC v. Rubyy, LLC, 2009 WL 3762418, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 9, 2009) 
17   (“Rubyy’s eight-month delay, when considered in conjunction with the specific circumstances of 
18   this action—including the nature of the previous representation, the prejudice to Skyy, and 
19   Rubyy’s willingness to deal with Attorney Kinnear in settlement negotiations—weighs heavily 
20   against disqualification.” (emphasis added)); Openwave Sys. Inc. v. Myriad France S.A.S., 2011 
21   WL 1225978, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 31, 2011) (finding a four month delay unreasonable); 
22   Chartwell Staffing Servs. Inc. v. Am. Int’l Indus., Inc., 2021 WL5927845, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 
23   10, 2021) (finding a three-month delay unreasonable); Finmeccanica S.p.A. v. Gen. Motors Corp., 
24   2008 WL 11340060, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Apr. 29, 2008) (finding a six-month delay unreasonable).   
25        In the instant action, Defendants’ delay is significant.  As recounted above, much has 
26   happened since Baker Botts, and specifically Mr. Guy, began representing QuickLogic.  At no 
27

1   time during the initial filing of this action or the earlier motions to dismiss did Defendants express 
2   a concern about a possible conflict with Baker Botts’ representation of QuickLogic.  Baker Botts 
3   has put time and effort into defending Plaintiff against a motion to dismiss and has developed a 
4   strong understanding of the facts at hand.  Disqualifying Baker Botts at this point would prejudice 
5   QuickLogic.                                                           
6        Because an attempt to disqualify the opposing attorney is often tactically motivated and 
7   disruptive to the litigation process, disqualification is a drastic measure that is generally 
8   disfavored.  See Visa U.S.A., Inc. v. First Data Corp., 241 F. Supp. 2d 1100, 1104 (N.D. Cal. 
9   2003).  Given the unlikelihood that an actual breach of confidentiality occured,3 the strategic 
10   timing of the motion (filed just days after Defendants’ motion to dismiss was denied), and the 
11   delay in filing, Defendants’ motion appears to be motivated by a desire to derail the ongoing 
12   litigation.  It is for this reason that motions for disqualification are “subjected to a particularly 
13   strict judicial scrutiny.”  Optyl Eyewear Fashion Int’l Corp. v. Style Cos., Ltd., 760 F.2d 1045, 
14   1050 (9th Cir. 1985).  The party seeking disqualification bears a “heavy burden,” which 
15   Defendants have failed to meet.  See City & Cnty. of S.F. v. Cobra Sols., Inc., 38 Cal. 4th 839, 851 
16   (2006).  For these reasons, Defendants’ motion to disqualify is DENIED.
